Which PFS sky lines vary together

RAGNAR now groups the lines whose intensity ratios stay fixed over all the skies it simulates, and finds the sections of spectrum that change linearly together. These are the groups and sections for the four PFS arms; the groups are tested on the sky spectra the LSFs were calibrated on.

Branch ragnar-new-2026 of astrockragh/RAGNAR · dev/covariation.py, pfs_covar/

What RAGNAR computes

Every spectrum of a RAGNAR run is one sky: here Trot 180 / 210 K, Tvib 8000 / 12000 K, hot population ×0.75 / 1 / 1.33, five chemistry draws, PWV 0 / 3 mm at ZD 30°, and three LSF widths (±5%), 360 skies per arm. For each pair of robust lines, Sij is the scatter of ln(Ii/Ij) over those skies, with I the line-only spectrum at the line centre (no centroider, no continuum). Sij = 0.01 means the ratio is fixed to 1%.

Lines are grouped by complete linkage at 1%, so every pair inside a group has Sij ≤ 1%. The four arms were run with the same grid and seed, so they simulate the same skies and lines can be grouped across arms. A group is a set of lines with a fixed ratio. Two thirds of the groups are one upper state (Λ-doublets, P/Q/R branches, and the same level in different bands); the rest join levels of one v′ whose rotational energies are close enough that Trot 180–210 K moves their ratio by less than 1%.

Against the PFS sky: b, r, n

The low-resolution data are four all-sky visits on two nights (2025-09-12 and 09-13), stacked per spectrograph. The Moon was 49° up and 72% full on night 1 and below the horizon on night 2, and the OH was about half as bright on night 2. For each line, di is the change of its ln amplitude from night 1 to night 2, averaged over the spectrographs. Lines that vary together keep their ratio, so di − dj = 0 within a group. The observed matrix is |di − dj|, on the same colour scale as Sij.

Amplitudes are measured the same way in the data and in RAGNAR's simulated spectra. The amplitude is the LSF Gaussian at the list wavelength, fitted within ±1σ, above a local baseline. The baseline is the mean of the faintest 30% of pixels between 2.5σ and 14σ on each side, joined by a straight line. So a smooth continuum in the data drops out, and RAGNAR's continuum is never used. The errors come from the scatter between the four spectrographs, which see the same sky (floor 1.0% in r and 3.5% in n per stack).

For flux calibration

  • Use lines from one RAGNAR group (covar_n ≥ 2) and measure them with a baseline taken from the data around each line. Require a peak of at least twice the baseline in every exposure. With that, groups held their ratios to 2% between two very different nights.
  • Lines with H₂O or O₂ absorption break groups even at high contrast. The fix4 grid only spans PWV 0–3 mm at one airmass. Drop flagged lines, or rerun the co-variation with a wider PWV and airmass grid.
  • The b groups are untested. On the moonlit night no b line in a group stood 2× above its baseline, and the blue ones (< 560 nm) changed by up to a factor of three. They need a dark night.
  • Groups that span arms measure the arms' relative response. Here r against n moved by between the nights.
  • The m data (six 60 s visits within 9 minutes) are noise-limited, and m was never observed with b, r or n. m groups and m-to-r groups are RAGNAR predictions for now.
from RAGNAR import ragnar
from dev.covariation import combine_covariation

# every run now adds upper_state, vgroup, covar_group, covar_n, covar_scatter, covar_nearest
# and writes {save_name}_{date}_covar.npz (per-sky intensities) next to the list
lineDf, *_ = ragnar(..., use_centroider = 0, covariation = True, covar_threshold = 0.01, save_name = 'sweep_0.112_0_r_fix4')

# group across runs that simulated the same skies (same grid, same seed)
T, S = combine_covariation(['lineLists/sweep_0.088_0_b_fix4_20261120_covar.npz', '..._r_...', '..._n_...', '..._m_...'],
                           names = ['b', 'r', 'n', 'm'], threshold = 0.01)

Sections that change linearly together

For calibration tests that need a stretch of spectrum in which every feature is the same in all skies up to one scalar multiplier per sky, the continuum aside. Each section is fitted as A(sky) × shape(λ). For every feature (one peak with its surroundings, between two minima of the mean spectrum) the residual is the rms over its pixels and all skies, divided by the rms of its own mean line spectrum. The worst feature is the largest of these in the section and has to be below the tolerance, so a bright line cannot carry other lines that change differently. Features with less than 2% of the section's line flux do not count: they are line wings and faint bumps between lines whose relative residual says nothing about the section. A section that one line dominates passes trivially (the 557.7 nm region in b), so the tables count the features that do count. The whole-window value is the same rms over all pixels at once, which bright features dominate. The skies are the 120 per arm at the nominal LSF (Trot, Tvib, hot population, chemistry and PWV vary), line-only. The split uses the fewest sections.

What these sections can and cannot carry

  • RAGNAR draws the chemistry of all species from one quantile, so OH, O₂, OI and Na move along one curve in the simulations. No section that passes mixes species (more than 2% of its line intensity from a second species), and I would keep it that way: real skies vary those species independently.
  • The fix4 grid has two values each of Trot and Tvib. A section is tested through the way the parameters combine, but curvature along a single parameter is not visible with two values. A denser grid (and independent species draws) would make the sections safer for a test on many exposures.
  • A continuum that is the same in every exposure only shifts the intercept. A changing one (moonlight, twilight) adds a second pattern in real data, so subtract a local baseline first or give the continuum its own term.
  • The LSF is held at its nominal width. If the test spans LSF changes (fibres, spectrographs), a single feature stays linear but neighbours can stop following each other.
  • Two sky states are enough to test it: a shape change between them is visible. The 5–10 nm windows below are tested on the PFS data.

5–10 nm windows, model and data

Every window 5–10 nm wide with edges at minima of the mean spectrum, holding at least 1% of the arm's line flux and at most 10% of its line intensity in H₂O or O₂ absorption. The test is the one above: every feature the same up to one scalar per sky. The model number spans RAGNAR's 120 skies. The data number is the same measure for what was observed. Per spectrograph, each exposure is fitted as A × one common line shape, plus a linear continuum (not part of the test) and a small wavelength shift; the residual has the noise taken out.

Over RAGNAR's 120 skies no 5–10 nm window is the same up to a scalar to better than about 7% in its worst counted feature: any window that wide spans several rotational levels, and Trot 180–210 K moves their ratios. Between the two observed nights, which differ less than the grid, the best windows changed by 2–5% in the worst feature and 1.4–2.2% over the whole window, against 0.2–1.2% within a night. The m data (9 minutes, 60 s visits) show no change beyond the noise in any window, so they test nothing. Over the full m arm the best window is the same 7-3 P-branch stretch as in r, 883.2–892.7 nm (model 6.9% worst, 3.0% whole window), which the r data test below covers.
